current.headline: Understanding は: the Japanese topic marker
current.summary: It is written ha but said wa, and it may be the most useful little word in Japanese. Here is what は really does, and why English has nothing quite like it.

text.t: One of the first things you meet in Japanese is the particle
. It is written with the hiragana for
ha
, but when it works as a particle it is always pronounced
wa
. That spelling is a leftover from older Japanese, and every learner trips over it once.
So what does it do? In short,
announces the topic: the thing you are about to say something about. Think of it as saying "As for…" before you get to the point.
As for me…
Here is the sentence almost every learner says first.
Read literally, it says "As for me, student is." Japanese puts the topic first, then the comment about it, and finishes with
to say "that's how it is". You learnt
in the previous lesson;
simply tells the listener what the
is about.

note.t: is a polite title that goes after a name. Never use it for yourself.

text.t: The topic does not have to be the subject
This is where
differs from anything in English. The topic is not always the person doing something. It can be almost anything you want to talk about, and the rest of the sentence comments on it.

note.t: is just the topic: as for today, rain.

text.t: Topics carry over
Once a topic is set, Japanese happily leaves it out of the next sentences. Both speakers know what is being discussed.
Alice does not repeat

in every sentence is one of the quickest ways to sound like a textbook.
In casual speech a question is often just a statement said with a rising voice, and
is dropped. You will learn the polite question marker
in Stage 3.
